audits.mathematicalReason: Let F be the perpendicular foot of C on AB and let CF = h. The segment from A to the far-right lower vertex has horizontal span 2 and vertical span 1, so similarity gives AF = 2h. The segment from B to the bottom-left vertex has horizontal span 1 and vertical span 2, giving FB = h/2. Thus 1 = AF + FB = 5h/2, so h = 2/5. The triangle's area is (1/2)(1)(2/5) = 1/5. The assessed triangle-area scope fits, and both listed routes validly determine the height as alternative methods.

figureEvidence.fact: The three squares form an L: two across the top and one below the upper-left square. A and B are the upper corners of the upper-left square, so AB = 1.

C is the intersection of the segment from A to the lower-right vertex of the upper-right square and the segment from B to the bottom-left vertex of the lower square. Their horizontal/vertical spans are respectively 2/1 and 1/2.

audits.mathematicalReason: Use the box [0,4] × [0,4] × [0,h]. Containment of the radius-2 sphere forces its horizontal center coordinates to be (2,2), and h ≥ 4. Corner unit-sphere centers have horizontal coordinates independently equal to 1 or 3 and vertical coordinates 1 or h−1. Equal distances to corresponding upper and lower centers force the large sphere's vertical coordinate to be h/2. External tangency gives center distance 3, hence 1² + 1² + (h/2−1)² = 9. Since h/2−1 > 0, h/2−1 = √7, yielding h = 2 + 2√7. Spatial distance matches the assessed scope. A plane through the two centers produces externally tangent great circles, so the circle-position support is defensible for this method.

figureEvidence.fact: The diagram shows four smaller spheres at the upper corners and four at the lower corners, surrounding one larger sphere. The apparent overlaps in the perspective drawing are not used as evidence of intersection.

audits.mathematicalReason: Place P1 at (0,0,0), its three adjacent vertices on the unit coordinate axes, and P1′ at (1,1,1). Equal edges of the triangular face near P1 force its vertices to be X1=(t,0,0), X2=(0,t,0), X3=(0,0,t), with side length s=√2t. The opposite equilateral face similarly has vertices Y1=(1−t,1,1), Y2=(1,1−t,1), Y3=(1,1,1−t), because its side length is also s. The cross-face edge X1Y2 has squared length 1+2(1−t)². Equating this to s²=2t² gives 3−4t=0, so t=3/4 and s=3√2/4. This value lies on the required unit segments. The selected spatial-distance assessment and coordinate/equilateral-triangle support fit this solution without asserting that coordinates are universally required.

figureEvidence.fact: The purple octahedron has three vertices on the cube edges incident to P1 and three on the edges incident to P1′. The displayed edges connect each group of three into a triangular face and connect nonopposite vertices across the two faces.

The cube labels identify P2, P3, and P4 as the three neighbors of P1 and each primed vertex as the opposite cube vertex. No intercept lengths are inferred from their apparent positions in the drawing.

audits.mathematicalReason: The original cube has side length 1 foot. The slab heights are a=1/2, b=1/3, c=1/17, and d=1−1/2−1/3−1/17=11/102. Separately, each 1×1×t slab has surface area 2+4t, so their total is 8+4(a+b+c+d)=12 square feet. In the depicted bottom-aligned order C–B–A–D, the glued areas are c, b, and d, whose sum is 1/17+1/3+11/102=1/2 square foot. Each interface removes two exposed copies, giving 12−2(1/2)=11 square feet. The simple-solid surface-area assessment and composite-solid support fit; summing exposed faces and subtracting glued interfaces are both valid routes.

figureEvidence.fact: The horizontal cuts produce slabs A, B, C, D from top to bottom, all with the original cube's unit-square footprint; the first three thicknesses are labeled 1/2, 1/3, and 1/17.
The reassembled slabs are side-by-side in order C–B–A–D with coplanar bottoms and common unit depth. Consequently, each glued interface has area equal to the smaller adjacent height times 1.

audits.mathematicalReason: Form a graph whose edges join pods without a walkway. The pods receiving grades 1 through 7, in that order, must form a path visiting every vertex of this complement graph. Its edges are AD, AE, BD, BE, BG, CG, DF, DG, EG. C and F each have degree 1, so they must receive grades 1 and 7 in some order. Taking C=1 and F=7 forces G=2 and D=6. A has only D and E as complement neighbors and is not an endpoint, so A=5 and E=4; the remaining pod B receives 3. Thus the order is C–G–B–E–A–D–F, or its reverse, and C+E+F=1+4+7=12 in either case. Graph translation, degrees, and path constraints directly match the assessed scope.

figureEvidence.fact: The walkway connections are AB, AC, AF, AG, BC, BF, CD, CE, CF, DE, EF, and FG. Each pair of boundary curves represents one walkway, not two graph edges; crossings without a pod do not create connections.

audits.mathematicalReason: Partition the hexagon into the three unit squares, triangle ABC, and gap triangles EAF, DBI, and GCH. At each central vertex, the two square angles and the equilateral triangle angle leave 360°−90°−90°−60°=120° for the gap. Each gap triangle therefore has two unit sides enclosing 120°. Its symmetry altitude gives two right triangles with hypotenuse 1 and a 30° angle, yielding gap base √3 and height 1/2, hence area √3/4. The central unit equilateral triangle also has area √3/4. Total area is 3+4(√3/4)=3+√3. Composite-area decomposition is the assessed operation, and every listed support node is applicable to the proposed elementary altitude calculation.

figureEvidence.fact: The three squares lie outside ABC, and their six outer vertices form the boundary D–E–F–G–H–I. The remaining interior gaps are triangles EAF, DBI, and GCH.
The squares share exactly the sides AB, BC, and CA with the central triangle, allowing their right angles and unit outer sides to determine the gap triangles. No regular-hexagon assumption is used.

audits.mathematicalReason: Set the lower-left corner at (0,0). The crossing segments join (1,5) to (7,0) and (0,4) to (8,1). Both have midpoint O=(4,5/2), so their intersection is the rectangle's center. Divide the upper-left shaded quadrilateral by the segment from the upper-left corner to O. The resulting triangles have areas (1/2)(1)(5/2)=5/4 and (1/2)(1)(4)=2, totaling 13/4. The lower-right shaded quadrilateral is its half-turn image, so the total is 13/2. The composite-area assessment, triangle-area support, and central-symmetry support all fit this method.

figureEvidence.fact: The top edge is split into lengths 1 and 7, and the bottom edge into 7 and 1. The left edge is split into 1 above and 4 below, while the right edge is split into 4 above and 1 below.

The two segments connect the indicated top/bottom points and left/right points. The shaded regions are the upper-left and lower-right quadrilaterals bounded by those segments and the rectangle's sides.

audits.mathematicalReason: Scale the common square side to 1. Along the horizontal line, take E=0, H=1, I=2; the midpoint conditions give D=1/2 and C=3/2. Extend AB to meet the line IJ at K. Then AK=3/2 and KJ=2, so right triangle AKJ has area 3/2. Rectangle BKIC has width 1/2 and height 1, hence area 1/2. Removing it leaves the shaded pentagon AJICB with area 1. The sum of the three square areas is 3, so the requested ratio is 1/3. The candidate's triangle-minus-rectangle decomposition is valid, and midpoint lengths, elementary areas, and the meaning of a ratio are appropriate support.

figureEvidence.fact: The two lower squares EFGH and GHIJ share side GH, with E, D, H, C, I collinear in that order. Square ABCD lies above this line.
The shaded boundary is A–J–I–C–B, with AJ as its diagonal boundary. The placement of AB and IJ permits completing the larger right triangle and subtracting the upper-right rectangle.
